procedural_history.originating_court: Special Magistrate, Anti-Corruption for Uttar Pradesh at Lucknow
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order, dated the 17th May, 1952, of the Special Magistrate, Anti-Corruption for Uttar Pradesh at Lucknow in Case No. 40 of 1951.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The case was appealed to the Lucknow Bench of Allahabad High Court as Criminal Revision No. 200 of 1952. The High Court upheld the decision of the Special Magistrate.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated the 5th May, 1953, of the Lucknow Bench of Allahabad High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal but reduced the sentence of imprisonment to the period already served.

directions: The sentence of imprisonment is reduced to the period already undergone.

issue.issue_text: Whether an offence under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code is made out if the public servant who accepts the illegal gratification is not actually in a position to perform, or does not intend to perform, the official act for which the bribe is taken.

facts: The appellant, a public servant employed in the Railway, was convicted under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code for accepting illegal gratification from a complainant.
The bribe was taken as a motive for getting the complainant re-employed in the Railway.
The appellant argued that the offence was not made out because he was not in a position to give a job to the complainant, nor was it shown that he had influence with any official who could.
law: The Court analyzed Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code, which criminalizes a public servant accepting illegal gratification as a motive for rendering service with any public servant.

The Court specifically relied on the fourth explanation to Section 161, which provides an example of a public servant committing the offence by inducing someone to erroneously believe they have influence and accepting money for that supposed service.
application: The Court rejected the appellant's argument, stating it was "without any substance."
It held that the gist of the offence is the acceptance of the illegal gratification by the public servant, not their ability to perform the promised act.

It is sufficient if the public servant who receives the money takes it by "holding out" that they will render assistance to the giver with another public servant, and the giver gives the money under that belief.

The Court clarified that it is irrelevant whether the public servant is actually capable of doing the act or even intends to do it. Even if the public servant is also guilty of cheating, they are "none the less" guilty of the offence under Section 161.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an offence under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code is made out even if the public servant who accepts the illegal gratification is not actually in a position to perform, or does not intend to perform, the official act. The core of the offence is the act of taking the bribe under the pretense of being able to influence an official act.

issue.issue_text: Whether the findings of fact by the lower courts were unsustainable and warranted interference in an appeal on special leave.

facts: The case was an appeal on special leave.
The appellant's counsel argued that the view taken by the lower courts on the evidence was unsustainable.
law: In an appeal on special leave, the Supreme Court will not interfere with the findings of fact from lower courts unless something "so seriously wrong" with those findings is demonstrated.
application: The Court noted that it was unnecessary to examine the appellant's argument regarding the evidence in detail because of the nature of the appeal (special leave).
The Court found that the appellant had not shown anything seriously wrong with the lower courts' findings of fact that would justify interference.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that since no serious error was shown in the lower courts' findings of fact, there was no reason to interfere with their decision in an appeal on special leave.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an offence under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code is made out if the public servant who accepts the illegal gratification is not actually in a position to perform, or does not intend to perform, the official act for which the bribe is taken.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that since he was not in a position to give the complainant a job, nor did he have influence with any official who could, the offence committed could only be cheating, not bribery under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, as adopted by the court, was that the actual ability or intent of the public servant to perform the promised act is irrelevant. The offence is constituted if the public servant accepts the illegal gratification by holding out that they will render assistance with another public servant, and the giver provides the money under that belief.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the findings of fact by the lower courts were unsustainable and warranted interference in an appeal on special leave.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the view taken by the lower courts on the facts of the case was unsustainable based on the evidence presented.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, as adopted by the court, was that in an appeal on special leave, the Supreme Court should not interfere with the lower courts' findings of fact unless something 'so seriously wrong' with them is demonstrated.

statutes.act_name: Indian Railway Establishment Code, Volume I (1951 Edition)

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The constitutional and statutory requirement that a public servant not be removed by an authority subordinate to the one by whom they were appointed is satisfied if the removing authority is of the same rank or grade as the appointing authority. These provisions do not imply that the removal must be by the very same authority who made the appointment or by their direct superior.
obiter: The gist of the offence under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code is the receipt by a public servant of illegal gratification as a motive or reward for the abuse of official position or function.
In an appeal on special leave, the Supreme Court will not interfere with findings of fact unless something seriously wrong is shown.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The offence of bribery under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code is constituted by the receipt of illegal gratification by a public servant as a motive or reward for abusing their official position. It is not necessary for the court to consider whether the public servant was actually capable of doing, or intended to do, the official act for which the bribe was taken. Furthermore, in an appeal on special leave, the court will not interfere with the findings of fact made by lower courts unless something "so seriously wrong" with them is demonstrated.
legal_tests_applied: The test for an offence under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code is whether a public servant received illegal gratification as a motive or reward for the abuse of official position or function, either by the receiver or by another public servant at their instance.

The standard for interfering with findings of fact in an appeal on special leave is whether the appellant has shown that there is something "so seriously wrong" with the findings that it calls for interference.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that he could not be guilty of bribery because he was not in a position to perform the official act was rejected, as the court held that the public servant's capability or intent to perform the act is irrelevant to the offence. The court stated, "When a public servant is charged under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code, and it is alleged that the illegal gratification was taken by him for doing or procuring an official act, it is not necessary for the Court to consider whether or not the accused as public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act."

The appellant's challenge to the lower courts' findings of fact was dismissed because he failed to meet the high threshold required for the Supreme Court to intervene in such matters on an appeal by special leave. The court found that "nothing so seriously wrong with the findings of fact have been shown, which call for interference by this".
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position prevailed because the court affirmed that the core of the offence under Section 161 is the corrupt act of accepting the bribe, not the ability to follow through. The court defined the crime as follows: "The gist of the offence under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code (in so far as it is relevant here) is the receipt by a public servant of illegal gratification as a motive or reward for the abuse of official position or function, by the receiver himself or by some other public servant at his instance."

The respondent's position on the factual findings was upheld because the court adhered to its procedural standard of not interfering with the factual determinations of lower courts in a special leave appeal unless a grave error is demonstrated.
